meta.case_name: Refinery in the Country of Georgia

prompt.context: It is 2012 and your client is one of the largest retailers of oil products in the country of Georgia (Eastern Europe). The company is exploring the idea to build a crude oil refinery in Georgia and has hired you to evaluate the idea. The goal of the company is to understand what the capacity of the refinery should be and to make a go/no-go decision.
prompt.question: What should the refinery's capacity be, and should the client proceed with building the refinery? Please structure your approach and walk me through your analysis.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's current market position?
clarifying_info.a: The company controls roughly 25% of all oil product sales in Georgia.

clarifying_info.q: Are there existing refineries in Georgia?
clarifying_info.a: Currently there are no crude refineries in Georgia. All refined oil products are imported from other countries.

clarifying_info.q: What oil products should we consider?
clarifying_info.a: For simplicity, consider three major oil products: Gasoline, Diesel, and Other Oil Products.

clarifying_info.q: How much crude oil does Georgia produce?
clarifying_info.a: Georgia produces 100,000 tons of crude oil annually and this number is projected to stay stable. All this crude is currently exported to foreign countries.

clarifying_info.q: Can the client import crude oil?
clarifying_info.a: The possibility of importing crude oil from neighboring countries is limited. Importing from countries further away is associated with high transportation costs.

clarifying_info.q: What does an oil refinery do?
clarifying_info.a: An oil refinery is a plant where the input is crude oil and the output is final products ready for retail consumption, such as gasoline, diesel, etc.

exhibits.title: Crude Oil Production and Oil Products Consumption in Georgia
exhibits.shows: Two tables: (1) annual crude oil production in Georgia from 2010 to 2014 (with 2013 and 2014 projected), and (2) oil products consumption in Georgia by product type for 2012 and 2013. Also includes three industry fact bullet points about crude oil export, import limitations, and retail pricing.

industry_facts: All crude oil produced in Georgia is exported. Oil producers are forced to sell at low prices due to small amounts and associated transportation costs.
The possibility of importing crude oil from neighboring countries is limited. Importing from countries further away is associated with high transportation costs.
All oil products are imported in Georgia. Due to high transportation costs, local retail prices are extremely high.

exhibits.title: Expected Output from Georgian Crude Oil and Wholesale Prices
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing the percentage breakdown of output products from Georgian crude oil refining, and a table of wholesale prices per ton for each oil product in Georgia.

framework: Identify this as an investment (go/no-go) case requiring both quantitative and qualitative analysis
Quantitative — determine refinery capacity based on available raw material supply
Quantitative — project revenues: output volumes by product type x wholesale prices
Quantitative — project costs: CapEx (construction), fixed costs (labor, overheads), variable costs (crude oil input)
Quantitative — build NPV model: EBIT(1-t) / discount rate minus initial investment
Qualitative — assess risks, assumption weaknesses, and other factors (raw material availability, demand, price volatility, competitive dynamics)
Synthesize into a go/no-go recommendation with key risks and next steps

questions.prompt: What should the refinery capacity be, and why?
questions.guidance: The candidate should use Exhibit 1 to observe that Georgia produces ~100,000 tons of crude oil annually (stable projection), and that importing additional crude is severely limited by transportation costs. Therefore the refinery capacity should be set at 100,000 tons — the full domestic crude output. The candidate should also note that 100,000 tons is roughly 10% of total Georgian consumption (~940,000 tons in 2013), and that high transportation costs on imports mean there will be sufficient local demand for domestically refined products.

math.setup: Total domestic crude available = ~100,000 tons/year (stable). Total oil products consumed in Georgia (2013) = 400,000 + 500,000 + 40,000 = 940,000 tons. Refinery output as % of consumption = 100,000 / 940,000 ≈ 10.6%.
steps: No meaningful crude import possible → capacity constrained to 100,000 tons
100,000 tons / 940,000 tons total consumption ≈ 10% — a meaningful but not dominant share
High import transportation costs mean local refinery products can be priced competitively
math.answer: Refinery capacity should be 100,000 tons per year.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate total annual revenue from the refinery.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the output percentage breakdown from the pie chart to the 100,000-ton capacity to get output volumes per product, then multiply by the respective wholesale prices to get revenue per product and total revenue.

math.setup: Total input: 100,000 tons crude. Output mix: 30% Gasoline, 50% Diesel, 15% Other Oil Products, 5% Loss. Prices: Gasoline $1,000/ton, Diesel $900/ton, Other $700/ton.

questions.prompt: Calculate the CapEx and annual operating costs for the refinery.
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm cost categories and break them into fixed and variable components. CapEx: construction cost. Fixed: labor, overheads. Variable: crude oil purchase cost. The company owns land so land cost is ignored.

math.setup: Capacity: 100,000 tons. CapEx: $500,000 per 1,000 tons. Labor: 1 employee per 1,000 tons at $20,000/year. Overheads: 10% of total revenue. Crude oil variable cost: $600/ton.

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of the refinery investment. (Discount rate: 10%, Tax rate: 20%, no depreciation, perpetuity assumption.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate EBIT, apply tax to get after-tax income, divide by discount rate for perpetuity value, then subtract initial CapEx investment. The simpler perpetuity approach (NPV = EBIT(1-t)/r - CapEx) is preferred over a full FCF model for this case.

math.setup: Revenue = $85,500,000. Total costs = $70,550,000. EBIT = Revenue - Costs. Tax rate = 20%. Discount rate = 10%. CapEx (initial investment) = $50,000,000. Perpetuity: no growth, year 1 cash flows repeat forever.
math.answer: NPV = $69,600,000 (strongly positive — project appears financially attractive)

brainstorming.prompt: The NPV looks very attractive. What are the key risks, weaknesses in the assumptions, and other qualitative factors the client should consider before making the final go/no-go decision?

categories.name: Raw Material Supply Risk
ideas: Georgian crude production is only ~100,000 tons and projected stable — but actual production could decline
Oil producers currently export all crude; the client will need to negotiate domestic supply contracts at competitive prices
If producers prefer to continue exporting (better prices elsewhere), raw material availability is not guaranteed

categories.name: Demand and Market Risk
ideas: 100,000 tons is ~10% of Georgian consumption — demand exists, but the client must secure distribution
Competing imports may undercut local refinery prices if global oil prices shift
Client has 25% market share in retail but must still win customers for locally refined product

categories.name: Price and Macro Risk
ideas: Oil prices are highly volatile — the $600/ton crude input price and output prices used could shift materially
The model assumes prices are stable in perpetuity — unrealistic for a commodity business
Exchange rate fluctuations could affect import cost competitiveness

categories.name: Financial / Model Assumption Weaknesses
ideas: Perpetuity model with no growth overstates or understates value depending on outlook
Depreciation was ignored — in reality capex depreciation would reduce taxable income and affect cash flows
No working capital changes modeled
10% discount rate may not reflect actual country risk premium for Georgia (emerging market)

categories.name: Operational and Regulatory Risk
ideas: Building and operating a refinery is complex — construction delays and cost overruns are common
Environmental regulations and permitting could delay or block construction
Skilled labor availability for refinery operations in Georgia may be limited
No existing refinery industry in Georgia means lack of local expertise and supply chain

categories.name: Strategic and Competitive Risk
ideas: First-mover advantage, but also first-mover risk — no proven model in Georgia
Potential for competing refinery investment if this one succeeds
Long-term energy transition risk (EVs, reduced fuel demand) may shorten payback horizon

recommendation: Proceed with the refinery investment — the NPV of ~$69.6M on a $50M investment is strongly positive, suggesting the project creates significant value
Set refinery capacity at 100,000 tons per year, aligned with Georgia's stable domestic crude production and constrained import options
risks: Oil price volatility could significantly erode margins — the model is sensitive to both crude input costs and refined product prices
Raw material supply is not guaranteed — crude oil producers currently export everything and must be contracted
The perpetuity / no-growth assumption is optimistic; the project's value is highly sensitive to discount rate and long-term demand
Country risk in Georgia (political stability, regulatory environment) adds uncertainty not captured in the base model
next_steps: Conduct sensitivity analysis on oil price assumptions (crude cost and product prices) to stress-test the NPV
Negotiate preliminary supply agreements with Georgian crude oil producers to secure raw material
Engage local regulatory authorities to understand permitting requirements and timeline
Refine the financial model to include depreciation, working capital, and a more realistic capital structure
Assess operational requirements — staffing, technology partnerships, construction contractors
